h1: Stewarding at a beer competition and what it teaches you
title: Stewarding at a Beer Competition | Craft Beer School
desc: What a beer competition steward does, how to volunteer and what you learn about tasting, judging and beer quality from the other side of the table.
teaser: Stewards carry bottles, pour samples and keep things running. They also hear every word the judges say.
standfirst: Stewarding is the easiest way into the world of beer judging. You help the competition run and in return you get a front row seat to how experienced judges taste, talk and score.
sections:
A beer competition needs more than judges. Someone has to receive the entries, sort them, keep them cold, bring them to the right table in the right order, open and pour them and collect the scoresheets. Those people are stewards.

Most stewards are volunteers. Many are beer lovers or homebrewers who want to learn more about judging. You do not need any qualification, only reliability and attention to detail. Our guide to how beer judges score explains what happens at the table you will be serving.

• Before judging: unpacking entries, checking labels against the entry list and sorting bottles into flights by style.
  • Keeping beer cold: entries wait in fridges or cold rooms and come out in small batches, so they reach the table at the right temperature.
  • At the table: bringing out each entry in order, opening it, pouring samples for each judge and keeping the bottle out of sight.
  • Paperwork: handing out scoresheets, collecting them and checking that each one has an entry number, a score and the judge's details.
  • Tidying: clearing glasses, refilling water and crackers and keeping the area quiet.

The most important rule is that judging stays blind. Judges see only an entry number, never a brand or a brewer's name. A good steward makes sure no label, cap or box gives the beer away.

Judges taste a flight of similar beers one after another. If entries arrive out of order, warm or badly poured, the judging suffers. A beer poured carelessly can lose its head and carbonation before the judges smell it. A strong beer served before a delicate one can numb the palate.

So stewards learn to pour gently down the side of the glass and then straighten up to build a modest head. They learn to keep the flight in the order the head judge asks for, often from lighter to stronger. These small habits make the result fairer for every entrant.

This is the real reward. At the table you hear experienced judges describe beers in detail: the aroma, the malt and hop balance, the yeast character, the finish and the faults. You hear them explain why a beer scored 38 rather than 30 and how they suggest the brewer fix it.

If the judges are happy for you to taste, take a small sample and compare your impressions with theirs. You will quickly notice the gap between "I like this" and "this has a clean malt base with light diacetyl in the finish". Closing that gap is what learning to judge means. Do this only when invited, keep tastes tiny and remember that stewards are working, so drink water and stay sharp.

When you collect scoresheets, glance at how they are written. Good scoresheets describe what the judge found, explain how it fits or departs from the style and give one or two practical suggestions. Our guide to the BJCP scoresheet walks through each section.

If you brew, this is useful later. When you enter your own beers, you will understand what judges are looking for and how to read the feedback you get.

Competitions announce calls for stewards through homebrew clubs, brewing associations and social media. Reply early, because organisers plan numbers in advance. Be clear about when you can attend and stick to it. Arrive on time, wear closed shoes and plan to be on your feet for most of the day.

Tell the organisers if you want to learn judging. Many will place you with an experienced judge who is happy to explain things.

Many judges started as stewards. After a few competitions you will know whether you want to go further. The next step is usually a formal judging programme such as the BJCP. Our guide to the BJCP exam explains how it works.

Even if you never judge, stewarding sharpens your tasting and gives you a better understanding of beer quality. The thing it cannot give you is structured practice on specific faults, where you taste a known fault side by side with a clean sample until you can name it without hesitation.
faqs: Do I need beer knowledge to be a steward?
No. Organisers look for reliable volunteers who can follow instructions. You will learn a lot about beer during the day.
Sometimes, if the judges and organisers allow it. Keep samples very small, because you are working and need to stay alert.
Is stewarding a step towards becoming a judge?
Yes. Many judges started as stewards. It is a good way to learn how judging works before taking a formal programme.
